Q: Error "can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes" A:

I wanted to compare the local naive datetime with an aware datetime from a timeserver. I basically created a new naive datetime object using the aware datetime object. It's a bit of a hack and doesn't look very pretty, but it gets the job done.

import ntplib
import datetime
from datetime import timezone

def utc_to_local(utc_dt):
    return utc_dt.replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc).astimezone(tz=None)

try:
    ntpt = ntplib.NTPClient()
    response = ntpt.request('pool.ntp.org')
    date = utc_to_local(datetime.datetime.utcfromtimestamp(response.tx_time))
    sysdate = datetime.datetime.now()

...here comes the fudge...

    temp_date = datetime.datetime(int(str(date)[:4]),int(str(date)[5:7]),int(str(date)[8:10]),int(str(date)[11:13]),int(str(date)[14:16]),int(str(date)[17:19]))
    dt_delta = temp_date-sysdate
except Exception:
    print('Something went wrong :-(')

Q: Removing a public @Override method and binary compatibility A:

Yes and no; it depends. Mostly: Yes, this change will probably be binary backwards compatible.

Context

A few scenarios where it'd be a no:


// Assume we have:

class Parent<T> {
  Number yell() { System.out.println("HEY!"); return 5; }
  void example(T arg) {}
}

class Child extends Parent<String> {
  Integer yell() { System.out.println("HEYHEY!"); return 10; }
  void example(String arg) {}
}

Then:

  • Any code that treats an expression of type Child as a Parent for some reason would be allowed, of course, to invoke foo.yell(). Even if foo is pointing at an instance of Child, if you remove yell() from Parent, that could would no longer work. For example, ((Parent) child).yell()would compile before the change, would not compile after the change, and any code compiled before the change would no longer execute if you change justParent.class`.

  • Child has a hidden synthetic method with signature void example(Object arg) which passes through to example(String arg), in order to 'override' Parent's example(T arg) whose signature is example(Object) (because T erases to Object here). In various scenarios you can run into trouble; in particular, if you recompile Child with the updated Parent (i.e. one without example(T arg) in), and you try to execute a newly compiled Child with an oldly compiled Parent, weird things can happen (that would result in NoSuchMethodError).

  • Child has a hidden synthetic method with signature Number yell() which passes through to Integer yell().

The thing about synthetic methods is: synthetic methods at the source code method act like they do not exist; attempting to compile code that invokes a synthetic produces the same errors as if that method didn't exist at all. At the class file level, however, synthetic methods act exactly like non-synthetics; any INVOKEVIRTUAL to a synthetic method works just fine. That's the point of them. The upside is: The only code you have to worry about is code that was compiled for your Child and Parent as they are now (before you make this change), invoking one of the synthetics.

Conclusions

  • Your question is too broad to give a definitive answer; it depends on the nature of these methods and exactly which mix of class files you end up running.

  • You can use javap and a bit of a script to go dig for calls you know will fail if you make this change - any INVOKEVIRTUAL to any sig that poofs out of existence. You know what you're looking for: It's easy enough to search the javap output for INVOKEVIRTUAL to Parent.yell or Child.yell with any signature (i.e. in the above, be it ()Ljava/lang/Number;, (Ljava/lang/Object;)V - doesn't matter), make an inventory of all variants in all class files you intend to remain backwards compatible (cook up a bunch of examples if you do not have a full accounting of all code that uses this code, for example if you've written an open source library), apply your change, check which signatures disappeared, then check your list if any of the inventoried code INVOKEVIRTUALs any of them. If the answer is yes: Voila, those aren't binary compatible. If the answer is no: Voila, it's all good.

The JVM is 'simple'. Any INVOKEVIRTUAL instruction has a specific target (a specific type name + a specific method name + an exact signature) and the JVM does not play games: Either that exact method exists and the INVOKEVIRTUAL will work, or it does not, and it'll fail.

Q: Eclipse - Target "unknown" in Android device chooser A:

When the phone is plugged in and the Eclipse window shows the "Unknown" icon..., on the phone turn off USB Debugging and then on again.

It will then ask to allow that computer to connect, and you can say to always let it do so. Then it comes up OK.
